problem: Explanation methods (attention, gradient) were developed for single-step classification and had never been evaluated on VLN models; different methods give different word rationales, and naive erasure at a single step is confounded by history that already encodes the erased words.
motivation: Knowing which instruction words a VLN agent actually uses is needed to diagnose and debug it, but explanations are only useful if faithful. VLN is sequential, so faithfulness metrics must account for historical textual and visual information; otherwise erasure results do not reflect true word importance at a step.
key_idea: Evaluate step-wise textual explanations for VLN by erasing or preserving top-k words in the instruction from the start, forcing the agent to replay its original actions up to step t, then measuring decision flips and probability changes at step t.
insight: Across both models and both datasets, Integrated Gradients is the most faithful method, which the authors attribute to it handling gradient saturation; attention-based methods (VaAtt, VecNorm) are clearly less faithful. Comparing IngGrad with human rationales (R2R): keeping the human words changes 36.3%/39.8% of Rec-VLN-BERT decisions, while erasing them flips only 34.8%/36.7%. So the models partly agree with humans but also rely on other tokens. Results on RxR are higher than on R2R, partly because the erased-token rate is higher (23% vs 13%).
method: Replay-based erasure pipeline: erase or preserve top-k tokens of the instruction at the start, force the agent to take the original actions a_1..a_{t-1} so observations match the original run, then compare the step-t decision and probabilities.

Faithfulness metrics: COMP (probability drop after erasing top-k), SUFF (probability drop when keeping only top-k), DFw/oR (decision flip rate after erasing), DFw/R (decision flip rate when keeping only the rationale).

Explanation methods benchmarked: attention-based (Vanilla Attention, Vector Norms extended to general attention modules) and gradient-based (Vanilla Gradient, Gradient x Input, GradCAM, Integrated Gradients with an empty padding-token baseline).
OOD mitigation: results are averaged over Slice Out (delete tokens) and Token Replacement (MASK for transformer, UNK for RNN).
Choice of k: the average human rationale length from LA-R2R (4 tokens) and Landmark-RxR (25/26 tokens).
Human comparison: on steps common to expert and predicted paths, the same number of tokens as the human rationale is erased or preserved for IngGrad versus the human annotation.

setting.backbone: Rec-VLN-BERT (transformer) and EnvDrop (RNN), both trained models used as the subjects of explanation
setting.training_data: R2R and RxR (English subset) training sets; R2R Rec-VLN-BERT weights taken from released checkpoint, the others trained by the authors
setting.observation: Panoramic view (36 views) with navigable candidate views and the instruction
setting.privileged: Human-annotated step-wise rationales (LA-R2R, Landmark-RxR) used to set k and for comparison; expert paths used in the human comparison

numbers_note: The paper is an explanation benchmark. Its main results are faithfulness metrics (DFw/oR, COMP, DFw/R, SUFF) for each explanation method in Tables 3-4. The best, IngGrad on Rec-VLN-BERT R2R val-unseen, gets DFw/oR 48.1, COMP 34.3, DFw/R 31.1, SUFF 21.3. On RxR val-unseen it gets 73.4, 56.4, 23.4, 12.0. These are not navigation SR/SPL, so only the models' navigation performance is listed above.
results: IngGrad is the most faithful explanation method for Rec-VLN-BERT on both R2R and RxR (R2R val-unseen DFw/oR 48.1%, RxR val-unseen 73.4%). For EnvDrop, IngGrad and GradInp are comparable. Attention-based methods are consistently the least faithful. IngGrad also beats human-annotated rationales in faithfulness (R2R val-unseen Rec-VLN-BERT DFw/oR 49.1% vs 36.7% for humans).
limitations: Only textual explanations from two attention-based and four gradient-based methods are evaluated; propagation-based methods and visual explanations are not covered.
Only two VLN models (Rec-VLN-BERT, EnvDrop) are studied; erasure-based evaluation may suffer OOD effects, and GradInp's strong result on EnvDrop is left unexplained.
